section_summary: This section contains diplomatic correspondence, consular despatches, memoranda, and telegrams from 1930 to 1939 relating to Japanese Emperor Hirohito, focused primarily on the annual exchange of official birthday greetings between President Franklin D. Roosevelt and the Emperor. It also documents diplomatic sensitivities and friction over American press depictions of the Emperor, including Japanese objections to a feature in Life magazine and efforts by the Japanese Consul General in Singapore to suppress copies of Ken magazine containing an objectionable caricature. In addition, the section includes reports on anti-foreign ideology ('Sonno Joi') promoted in Japanese-ruled Korea, extensive celebrations and economic appeals by the Japanese community in Peru on the Emperor's 37th birthday, and consular courtesies exchanged in Sumatra in 1930.

subfiles.about: Consul Thomas McEnelly reports on the Japanese Consul General's attempts to buy up an issue of 'Ken' magazine caricaturing the Emperor and details his controversial conduct in Singapore.
subfiles.from: Thomas McEnelly, American Consul, Singapore
subfiles.summary: American Consul Thomas McEnelly in Singapore submits Despatch No. 418 reporting that Japanese Consul General I. Okamoto visited the Consulate General after receiving cable instructions from Tokyo to buy up all copies of the April 1938 debut issue of the American magazine 'Ken'. The magazine contained an objectionable cartoon entitled 'Plagues' depicting Emperor Hirohito alongside Hitler, Mussolini, and Franco. Okamoto noted that while serving as Consul in Seattle, he had previously initiated a diplomatic protest over an American cartoon of the Emperor. McEnelly also reports on Okamoto's contentious local behavior, including bringing uninvited Japanese players to the British-controlled Singapore Golf Club and demanding honorary consular membership, as well as reports from British military intelligence head Lt. Col. Hayley-Bell that Okamoto had attempted to bribe Singapore newspaper editors with costly Japanese gifts. The despatch is preserved in the file in multiple copies, including ordinary mail and air mail versions.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 418 on Objectionable Cartoon of Japanese Emperor in Ken Magazine and Activities of Consul General Okamoto
subfiles.to: Cordell Hull, Secretary of State

subfiles.about: Consul General Homer Brett reports on celebrations of the Emperor's birthday by the Japanese colony in Peru, including appeals on civic loyalty and textile import quotas.
subfiles.from: Homer Brett, American Consul General, Callao-Lima, Peru
subfiles.summary: Consul General Homer Brett submits an extensive voluntary political report describing celebrations in Peru on April 29, 1938, commemorating the 37th birthday of Emperor Hirohito. The report includes full translations of prominent articles and advertisements published in Lima newspapers such as El Comercio and La Prensa. In an address entitled 'To Our Peruvian Friends', Sadajiro Yumoto, President of the Central Japanese Society of Peru, emphasizes traditional Japanese loyalty, cites the 1890 Imperial Rescript on Education of Emperor Meiji, and argues that Peruvian-born children of Japanese parents are loyal Peruvian citizens, though Brett notes Peruvian authorities refuse to recognize them as such or permit them to serve in the Peruvian military. The report also translates a detailed commercial study by R. Takahashi, President of the Japanese Association of Commerce and Industry, who presents Japanese foreign trade statistics for 1936 and 1937 and argues for the abolition of Peruvian quotas on Japanese cotton textiles. Brett concludes that Peruvian cotton manufacturers and authorities remain strongly committed to maintaining import quotas against Japanese competition.
subfiles.title: Voluntary Political Report: Celebration of Japanese Emperor's Birthday in Peru
subfiles.to: Cordell Hull, Secretary of State
